stimuli.text: A block of mass 6 kg on a 30° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 8 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.2. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.4 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.09\cos(10t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) and a hoop (I = MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.3 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A 0.3 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 60$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: That is the frequency.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
The ratio is m/k.
Include the 2π.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = 3t^3 + 2t^2 + 2t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 1$$ s?

options.why: Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.
Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.

questions.explanation: a(t) = 18t + 4, so at t = 1 the value is 22.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.8 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.
I = mL²/3.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 49 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 20 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Recheck the average.

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.04\cos(15t)$$ m. What is its maximum acceleration?

options.why: That is v_max.
Differentiate twice: Aω².
Correct. a_max = Aω².
Multiply by the amplitude.

questions.stem: A 77 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Include gravity.
Check the direction of the acceleration.
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).

questions.stem: A curve of radius 70 m is banked so that a car at 25 m/s needs no friction. What is the banking angle?

options.why: Measure the angle from the horizontal.
Use tan θ = v²/(rg), from dividing the force components.
Square the speed.
Correct. tan θ = v²/(rg).

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 100 N/m and 50 N/m are connected in parallel and support a 0.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Correct. k_eq = k₁ + k₂.
Both springs share the load.
The force is the weight, mg.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.

questions.stem: Masses of 8 kg and 3 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
Use T = m₂(g + a).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.

questions.stem: A car moving at 25 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 7 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

options.why: Divide by 2a, not a.
That is the stopping time in seconds.
Δx = v₀²/(2a).
Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0.

questions.stem: A 0.3 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds at 6 m/s. The contact lasts 0.04 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Divide by time.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Include the rebound.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 6x$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 2$$ m to $$x = 4$$ m?

options.why: The force is not constant.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 2 m down a 45° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.1. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Friction removes energy.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 19.5 m high at 6 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Take the square root for the time.
Fall time is √(2h/g).
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 150 m wide, moving at 8 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 4 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 250 kg load 21 m at constant speed in 17 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.
Correct. P = mgh/t.
P = W/t.

questions.stem: A planet has 2 times Earth's mass and 0.5 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: Correct. g ∝ M/R².
The ratio is inverted.
g decreases with radius.
g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.

questions.stem: A 5 kg cart moving at 5 m/s collides with and sticks to a 3 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
The carts share the momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 5·5/8 = 3.13 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 23.4 J.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 3.8 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Some energy goes into rotation.
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 2 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).
T² ∝ r³.
The exponent is 3/2.
Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 4 m down a 37° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction removes energy.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: A 4 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 1 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: I/R² = M/2.
For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 8.71 m/s².

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 440$$ N/m is compressed 0.23 m and launches a 0.8 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Take the square root.
The ½ appears on both sides.
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball on a 1.5 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle its speed is 8 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Centripetal force uses v².
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Include gravity.
Correct. At the top, T + mg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: A 2000 kg car heading east at 17 m/s collides with a 2500 kg car heading north at 17 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Divide by the total mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Weight each velocity by its mass.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 9 rad/s and amplitude 0.2 m. What is its speed when it is 0.08 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Use A² − x² under a square root.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.

questions.stem: Point masses of 3 kg and 4 kg are at the ends of a massless rod 1 m long. What is the rotational inertia about the rod's center?

options.why: Measure from the center, not an end.
Correct. Sum of mr² with r = L/2.
Each mass is L/2 from the center.
Square the distance.

questions.stem: A uniform 8 m beam weighing 500 N rests on supports at both ends. A 500 N load sits 1 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: Correct. Take torques about the left support.
The load is not at the center.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
That is the left support's force.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 4 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.3. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Friction opposes the motion.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Include friction on the table block.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 3x^3 - 36x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Take the square root.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 9x² − 36 = 0 gives x = 2 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A 5 kg ball moving at +6 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 3 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 3 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
That would be a sticking collision.
Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = 1.5 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 7.5 m/s.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 14 m/s at 70° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its horizontal range?

options.why: That is the maximum range, at 45°.
Use the full time of flight.
Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
Range uses sin 2θ.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 4.79 m/s, v₀y = 13.2 m/s. R = v₀² sin 2θ/g = 12.9 m.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 17 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 1$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 5 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
W = ½Iω².
Convert revolutions to radians.
½Iω² = W; solve for ω.

questions.stem: A 5 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 4t$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 3$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Divide by the mass to get speed.
Integrate the force over time.
The force is not constant.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 18 N·s; v = J/m = 3.6 m/s.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 1$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^2$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The rod is not uniform.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 8 kg and radius 0.4 m spins at 19 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 1.5 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
Use rotational inertias, not masses.
The clay's inertia is mR².
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 2.6 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.
τ = MgL/2.
Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
The weight acts at L/2.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$1 \times 10^{24}$$ kg and radius $$5 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.1 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.08$$ kg/s. What is its terminal speed?

options.why: Drag here is linear in v.
That is the time constant.
Solve mg = bv for v.
Correct. At terminal speed, mg = bv.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 12.3 m/s and τ = m/b = 1.25 s.

questions.stem: A 12 g bullet moving at 470 m/s embeds in a 1.2 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
h = V²/(2g).
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.

questions.explanation: V = 4.65 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 1.1 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 6 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.09 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
